title: Dipole Moments, Molecular Polarity and Polarisation

pages.title: Can a molecule have polar bonds but no overall polarity?

blocks.text: CO₂ contains polar C–O bonds, yet its overall dipole moment is zero. Water also has polar bonds, but its dipole is non-zero. The missing ingredient is molecular geometry.
A dipole is a separation of positive and negative charge. To combine several bond dipoles, we must consider their directions as well as their magnitudes.

pages.transition: Define the magnitude and direction of a charge separation.

pages.title: Define a dipole moment

blocks.text: For equal and opposite charges of magnitude Q separated by distance r, the dipole moment magnitude is μ=Qr. Use Q in coulombs and r in metres to obtain C m.
Chemists often use debye: 1 D=3.33564 × 10⁻³⁰ C m. Dipole moment is a vector quantity. Simply adding all bond-dipole magnitudes ignores cancellation.

Two equal pulls in opposite directions can cancel; pulls in different directions may leave a resultant. Dipole addition is a vector problem for the same reason. Looking only at how strong each bond dipole is misses the arrangement.

pages.transition: Use consistent charge and distance units in a numerical example.

pages.title: Calculate a simple dipole magnitude

blocks.text: Teacher-worked application: suppose separated charges each have magnitude 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and separation 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Then μ=Qr=1.00 × 10⁻²⁹ C m.
Convert to debye: μ=(1.00 × 10⁻²⁹)/(3.33564 × 10⁻³⁰) D≈3.00 D. These are illustrative charges and distance, not claimed measured values for a named molecule.

pages.transition: Apply vector cancellation to a symmetric linear molecule.

pages.title: Explain cancellation in carbon dioxide

blocks.text: CO₂ is linear with two equivalent C–O bonds pointing in opposite directions. Their dipoles have equal magnitudes and opposite directions, so the vector sum is zero.
The bonds remain polar individually. A zero molecular dipole therefore does not prove that every bond is non-polar; it may demonstrate geometric cancellation.

pages.transition: Compare that with bent and trigonal planar geometries.

pages.title: Explain water and boron trifluoride

blocks.text: Water is bent, so its two O–H dipoles do not cancel. BF₃ is trigonal planar with three equivalent bond dipoles separated symmetrically by 120°, whose vector sum is zero.
Compare the full arrangement, not merely the number of bonds. Two bonds can cancel when linear and identical, but fail to cancel when bent.

pages.transition: Lone-pair contributions make another instructive comparison possible.

pages.title: Compare ammonia and nitrogen trifluoride

blocks.text: NH₃ and NF₃ are both pyramidal. In the textbook’s qualitative model, N–H bond dipoles reinforce the lone-pair contribution, whereas N–F bond dipoles oppose it.
NF₃ consequently has a smaller net dipole moment even though F is more electronegative. Bond polarity alone cannot determine a polyatomic molecule’s net dipole without considering direction.

pages.transition: A different question concerns distortion of an ion’s electron cloud.

pages.title: An ionic bond can have covalent character

blocks.text: A positive ion can distort a neighbouring negative ion’s electron cloud. This distortion is polarisation. Electron density shifts towards the region between ions, adding covalent character to an otherwise ionic description.
The cation’s ability to distort is polarising power; the anion’s ease of distortion is polarisability. These terms refer to different partners in the same interaction.

pages.transition: Translate distortion into qualitative size and charge rules.

pages.title: Apply Fajans’ rules

blocks.text: A small, highly charged cation has strong polarising power. A large anion has a more easily distorted electron cloud. Both features favour greater covalent character.
For the same cation, iodide is generally more polarisable than fluoride. For the same anion, a smaller or more highly charged cation generally produces greater distortion.

pages.transition: Apply the rules while keeping the comparison partner fixed.

pages.title: Use two comparisons instead of one slogan

blocks.text: Compare LiCl and NaCl: Li⁺ is smaller, so it polarises Cl⁻ more strongly and LiCl has greater covalent character. Compare LiF and LiI: the larger I⁻ cloud is easier to distort, so LiI has greater covalent character.

The textbook also notes configuration effects: a cation with filled d electrons may shield less effectively than a noble-gas-type cation of similar size and charge. Compare all stated conditions, not charge alone.

Why does a large anion favour covalent character? Its outer cloud is more easily distorted by a cation, increasing density between the ions. This is a comparison of polarisability; it does not claim the anion’s formal charge changes during the comparison.

pages.transition: Separate molecular polarity from ionic polarisation in the final check.

blocks.text: Dipole moment measures charge separation and depends on vector addition. Polarisation describes distortion of one ion’s cloud by another, explaining covalent character in ionic compounds.
Use geometry for molecular dipoles and Fajans’ size/charge reasoning for ionic polarisation. A familiar name is less valuable than identifying which physical question the comparison asks.

questions.question: Why is CO₂ non-polar overall?
questions.answer: Its equal C–O bond dipoles cancel in a linear arrangement.

questions.question: Why do water’s bond dipoles not cancel?
questions.answer: Its bent geometry leaves a non-zero vector sum.

questions.question: Convert 6.67128 × 10⁻³⁰ C m to debye.
questions.answer: Divide by 3.33564 × 10⁻³⁰ C m per D to obtain 2.00 D.

questions.question: Why can NF₃ have a smaller dipole than NH₃?
questions.answer: The bond contributions oppose rather than reinforce the lone-pair contribution in the qualitative comparison.

questions.question: Which cation polarises a given anion more: Li⁺ or Na⁺?
questions.answer: Li⁺, because its smaller size gives greater polarising power.

questions.question: Which is more polarisable, F⁻ or I⁻?
questions.answer: I⁻; its larger electron cloud distorts more readily.

questions.question: Does zero molecular dipole imply all bonds are non-polar?
questions.answer: No. Symmetric cancellation of polar bonds can give zero net dipole.
